reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents an instructional discussion of affiliate marketing, including commission-based links, affiliate registration, advertising, and payment schedules. The affiliate and support links, along with a financial-advice disclaimer, are described as monetized educational context, and no deceptive request for money, credentials, or guaranteed investment returns is shown.

opening.argument: The video presents a low-barrier income pathway: register for an affiliate program, advertise products, and receive commissions when customers buy through the resulting link. The displayed workflow explicitly pairs “REGISTER,” “ADVERTISE,” and “GET PAID,” while showing a commission of up to 13% tied to customer orders within seven days. The speaker also directs viewers to affiliate links and explains that a referral code attributes the sale to them. This is not merely a discussion of commerce; it links a simple viewer action to a promised cash reward, with the key conditions controlled by an external platform.

citations.quote: Jumia offers an affiliate program that pays its affiliates up to 13% for recommending the products on the site.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this instructional does not remove the solicitation. The defense's quotes establish that commissions exist, but they do not establish that the proposed income is reliable, that eligibility and payment conditions are transparent, or that viewers can independently verify attribution. The practical conclusion is still an invitation to use the speaker's affiliate pathway, not neutral explanation alone.

citations.quote: I hope that you as a Kenyan content creator can start using affiliate links in your description.
you can get paid weekly bi-weekly or monthly depending on the site

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material describes ordinary performance-based advertising, not a payment for registration or a deposit. The commission is contingent on a customer buying a product, and the explanation expressly frames the link as a referral code used to attribute a sale. Nothing shown establishes deception, fabricated earnings, or a guaranteed return; the seven-day period is an attribution condition, not proof of fraud.

FINANCIAL DISCLAIMER The information contained on this video and this Channel is not intended as, and shall not be understood or construed as, financial advice.

opening.argument: Several risk signals are concentrated in one funnel. The material promotes external affiliate links, advertises earnings of up to 13%, and displays a seven-day window in which a customer's order can generate commission. The description also includes a crypto buying-and-selling link, while the speaker says payment may occur weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly. These claims create an appealing, apparently easy income opportunity whose conditions depend on clicks, purchases, tracking, and an outside platform. The combination deserves scam treatment because the promotional upside is prominent while the evidence does not demonstrate typical earnings, payment reliability, or meaningful safeguards.

citations.quote: Jumia offers an affiliate program that pays its affiliates up to 13% for recommending the products on the site.
Get started with crypto, buying and selling Bitcoins:
you can get paid weekly bi-weekly or monthly depending on the site

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense recasts the red flags as harmless context, but it does not answer their combination: an external link, an advertised percentage, a short attribution window, and recurring payment language. A disclaimer about financial advice does not verify the commission claim or explain whether the promoted crypto link is safe. The absence of a demonstrated loss is not evidence that the solicitation is trustworthy.

citations.quote: FINANCIAL DISCLAIMER The information contained on this video and this Channel is not intended as, and shall not be understood or construed as, financial advice.
when you go into the link and you click on the link and purchase within a set frame time

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are not promised investment returns or guaranteed income. The percentage is described as a commission for recommending products, and payment depends on a customer purchasing through an attributed link. The separate crypto link appears in the description, but the argument does not show that the video asks viewers to deposit, trade, or buy crypto. Risk language alone cannot establish a scam.

opening.argument: Although framed as education, the video functions as a recruitment and promotion pitch. It tells Kenyan creators they can make money without AdSense, supplies a Jumia affiliate link, demonstrates the affiliate dashboard, and ends by urging viewers to use affiliate links. The description repeats the commercial pathway and places multiple monetized links alongside the tutorial. The educational format therefore serves to move viewers toward registration, advertising, and tracked purchases, while presenting the opportunity in an unusually accessible way. That promotional role is more significant than the neutral label of “how it works.”

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense identifies genuine explanatory content but overlooks its behavioral endpoint. The speaker does not merely define affiliate marketing; he provides the signup route, describes the dashboard, and urges creators to adopt the links. Explaining mechanics can make a solicitation more persuasive, especially when the presentation foregrounds an answer to viewers who have not yet been monetized.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A call to use disclosed affiliate links is ordinary advertising instruction, not evidence of deception. The video explains that commissions arise only after a customer purchases, and the description identifies the affiliate program and includes a financial disclaimer. The argument shows promotion, but promotion of a real referral arrangement does not establish a scam without a false promise, hidden payment demand, or fabricated outcome.
